Prognostic impact—historic perspective of the evidence In 1985, Kennedy s . published a study of 73 asymptomatic, healthy individuals with frequent and complex ventricular ectopy who had been followed for 10 years, demonstrating prognoses comparable to those of the general population. 10 These findings were confirmed in a subsequent study by the same author 32 underscoring the continued interest in clarifying the prognostic implications of PVCs in healthy subjects. 33 Numerous studies published throughout the 1980s and 1990s produced conflicting results. A common criticism of these investigations was the insufficient application of rigorous diagnostic methods to exclude underlying cardiac disease. 34 In 1992, Kostis summarized the available evidence, concluding that PVCs do not independently contribute to mortality but may instead serve as markers of occult heart disease. 33 The adverse prognostic impact of PVCs is more evident in the presence of structural heart disease. Findings from studies conducted in the 1960s and 1970s were corroborated in subsequent decades, particularly among patients with prior ischaemic events. 35–38 Even in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, a relationship between PVCs and poor outcomes has been established. 39 , 40 In a 1993 review, 41 Myerburg et al . emphasized the role of PVCs in the pathophysiology of malignant arrhythmias, identifying them as the link between ischaemia and ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation. Meanwhile, the CAST trial demonstrated that suppression of ventricular ectopy with class I antiarrhythmic drugs in myocardial infarction survivors did not improve prognosis; on the contrary, patients treated with flecainide or encainide experienced higher mortality compared to those receiving placebo. 42 These findings reinforced the conclusion that PVCs are not independent contributors to mortality but rather markers of underlying disease. While the prognostic impact of PVCs in structural heart disease appears indisputable, evidence regarding their role in healthy individuals remains uncertain. Many studies reporting a negative impact relied solely on patient history to exclude structural disease and/or were conducted exclusively in male populations 12 , 43–48 . Among large population studies, Agarwal 49 demonstrated a higher incidence of heart failure (HF) in PVC patients compared with controls. Notably, the association between PVCs and incident HF was strongest in patients with fewer cardiovascular risk factors, with a six-fold increase in risk among those younger than 65 years without CHD, diabetes, hypertension, or atrial fibrillation. In a 12-year follow-up of Japanese men and women, 50 Hirose reported increased cardiovascular mortality among men with PVCs, whereas no prognostic impact was observed in women. More recent studies in Asian populations have again shown associations between PVCs and all-cause mortality, hospitalization, and HF at the population level. 48 , 51 Among the studies that incorporated echocardiographic evaluation at baseline, Dukes et al . 52 examined 1139 individuals whose PVC frequency was quantified by Holter monitoring. They found that individuals in the highest quartile of PVC frequency had a threefold risk of a five-year decline in LVEF, a 48% increased risk of incident CHF, and a 31% increased risk of death compared to those in the lowest quartile, after adjustment for confounders and a median follow-up of 13 years. Results were similar when PVCs were analysed as a continuous variable. In contrast, Lee et al 53 reported that only a small proportion of PVC patients with normal LVEF developed systolic dysfunction during approximately 5 years of follow-up.

Alongside studies demonstrating a negative prognostic impact of PVCs in the general population or in cohorts without apparent heart disease, others found no such association. Fisher 9 reported that the risk of coronary artery disease was not increased by the presence of PVCs on routine ECG in a cohort of factory workers aged 35–69. A decade later, Kennedy et al 10 published results from a 6.5-year follow-up of 73 asymptomatic, healthy subjects with frequent ventricular ectopy, reporting only one case of sudden death. Compared to the standardized mortality ratio, this suggested that long-term prognosis was not adversely affected by PVCs. This study contributed significantly to the view that PVCs are benign in the absence of structural heart disease, and several subsequent publications appear to confirm its findings. 53–58 In a study specifically focused on the potential development of Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC), Gaita et al 59 followed 61 patients with frequent right-ventricular PVCs. After an average follow-up of 15 years, no patient had died of SCD or developed ARVC, and half no longer exhibited PVCs. In a cohort of 5000 athletes, Verdile et al 60 observed that exercise-induced PVCs tended to resolve spontaneously or could be successfully treated, without affecting clinical outcomes.

Although studies reporting a negative prognostic impact of PVCs in subjects without apparent heart disease outnumber those showing no association, the overall evidence remains divided and inconclusive. This uncertainty is compounded by the fact that few studies consistently employed imaging diagnostics to exclude structural disease, relying instead on patient history. Meta-analyses addressing this issue were lacking until 2012, when Lee et al 61 published the first, followed shortly by Ataklte and colleagues. 62 Lee’s meta-analysis included studies with control populations based on adults without apparent heart disease, excluding unselected populations not evaluated for structural disease, studies of exercise-induced PVCs, and subgroup analyses within PVC cohorts. When multiple studies were based on the same cohort, only the most recent was included. Out of more than 3000 studies published between 1966 and 2011, only eight met these criteria, all of which were prospective observational cohort studies. Sensitivity analysis revealed that negative prognostic effects were observed primarily in male-only cohorts, while the single study incorporating echocardiography and exercise testing at baseline did not demonstrate worsened outcomes. According to the authors, heterogeneity among studies was substantial, and publication bias was not apparent. The pooled OR for death, cardiovascular death, SCD, or ischaemic heart disease was 1.72 (95% CI 1.28–2.31). Classic cardiovascular risk factors such as male gender, age, diabetes, and hypertension increased the odds of cardiovascular events, suggesting that patients with undetected structural disease were included, thereby influencing results. The authors concluded that if more advanced diagnostic techniques had been used to exclude structural disease, benign outcomes with PVCs would likely have been observed. Consistent with this, study quality assessment indicated that the increase in OR was less pronounced in higher-quality studies. Ataklte et al . included prospective cohort, nested case-control, and retrospective cohort studies, ultimately analysing 11 relevant investigations involving 106 000 patients. The prevalence of PVCs ranged from 1.2% to 10.7%, with mean follow-up times of 5–30 years. The six prospective studies showed no significant heterogeneity. The pooled RR for total cardiac death was 2.1 and the authors proposed two hypotheses: PVCs may trigger fatal ventricular arrhythmias, or they may represent markers of underlying disease (reverse causation). They also noted insufficient adjustment for confounders in some studies, though they did not emphasize the lack of diagnostic imaging as strongly as Lee et al.

More recent publications have continued to present conflicting evidence, with some studies suggesting a benign clinical course, 53 , 57 , 58 whereas others indicate a negative prognostic impact. 48 , 63 Two review articles recommend that patients with a low PVC burden and normal echocardiographic findings may be reassured, while those with a potentially significant burden or deemed at risk for cardiomyopathy should undergo regular clinical follow-up. 64 , 65 In a Japanese study based on retrospective data from an administrative database, 66 the frequency of PVCs, based on Holter monitoring, was not associated with clinical events, while the presence of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia was independently associated to heart failure incidence. A recent third meta-analysis, encompassing 25 studies, examined the relationship between PVCs and cardiovascular outcomes in populations without overt structural heart disease. 67 The analysis demonstrated that frequent PVCs were significantly associated with an increased risk of mortality, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and stroke. However, the authors emphasized that, according to the GRADE framework, the overall quality of evidence was rated as low. This assessment was primarily attributed to the observational nature of the included studies and methodological limitations, such as incomplete adjustment for clinically relevant confounders related to underlying heart disease. Additionally, concerns regarding residual confounding and selection bias, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings, were highlighted as further limitations. Some of the more recent studies investigating the prognostic impact of PVCs in healthy or apparently healthy subjects are summarized in Table 2 .

Meta-analyses have also examined exercise-induced PVCs. Kim et al, 69 analysed nine studies including 62 000 participants, finding that PVCs during recovery were associated with increased risk of death (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.22–1.96), whereas PVCs during exercise did not reach statistical significance (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.96–1.34). However, overall effects during exercise testing corresponded to an RR of 1.41 (95% CI 1.23–1.61) for all-cause mortality and 1.86 (95% CI 1.51–2.30) for cardiovascular mortality. Similar conclusions were reached by Lee et al . 70 in 2017, who found that only PVCs during recovery, not during exercise, were associated with poor prognosis. The authors suggested autonomic dysregulation, 71 , 72 with increased sympathetic drive creating a pro-arrhythmic substrate, as a possible mechanism leading to fatal outcomes.

Extra-cardiac clinical outcomes have also been investigated in relation to PVCs. Studies from Ofoma 73 and Agarwal 74 demonstrated an increased risk of ischaemic stroke among individuals with PVCs. A plausible explanation for this association is atrial fibrillation (AF), as the risk of developing AF has been shown to rise with increasing PVC incidence. 75 However, in studies where underlying structural disease was carefully excluded from the PVC population, no correlation with ischaemic stroke was observed. 76 Even in the absence of a prior diagnosis of stroke or transient ischaemic attack, central neurological symptoms have been linked to a high PVC burden (>10%). 77

PVC-induced cardiomyopathy When summarizing the evidence regarding the prognostic impact of PVCs in subjects without heart disease, PVC-induced cardiomyopathy (PVC-CM) must be considered separately since this entity, first described approximately 30 years ago, has a distinct pathophysiology. The earliest reports of PVC-CM were published in 1997 by Vijgen 78 and in 2000 by Chugh. 79 While Vijgen and colleagues described a patient with repetitive non-sustained ventricular tachycardia and dilated cardiomyopathy, in whom ablation of the arrhythmia focus led to recovery of ventricular systolic function, 78 Chugh’s paper was the first to directly associate cardiomyopathy with isolated, frequent PVCs, documenting recovery from heart failure after successful radiofrequency ablation. A few years later, Shiraishi published a similar case report 80 and recommended ablation as the treatment of choice in such patients. The pathophysiology of PVC-CM is likely distinct from the multiple mechanisms implicated in the broader impact of PVCs summarized thus far. Evidence for this distinction lies in the reversibility of PVC-CM, which is associated with a favourable prognosis when PVCs are effectively treated. It is possible that PVC-CM historically contributed to the general prognostic impact attributed to PVCs, particularly before the condition was formally described and before ablation techniques were established as effective therapeutic tools. 81 The mechanisms underlying PVC-CM remain incompletely understood, though several theories have been proposed. These include electromechanical dyssynchrony, extrasystolic potentiation, interpolation, R-R variability, and myocardial remodelling induced by short-coupled PVCs. 82 At the cellular level, suggested mechanisms involve altered myocardial perfusion and oxygen consumption, changes in ion channel and intracellular protein expression, and modifications in autonomic tone. 68 Dyssynchrony, in particular, has been highlighted as a possible pathophysiologic drive. 83 Reported prevalence of PVC-CM ranges from 6–7% in populations with frequent PVCs to as high as 38% in cohorts referred for ablation. 84

Although the body of evidence on PVC-CM and the positive effects of catheter ablation is growing, most studies linking PVCs to cardiomyopathy are retrospective or cross-sectional in design. 85 , 86 A meta-analysis focusing on characteristics associated with the risk of developing PVC-CM was published in 2022. 87 In total, 26 studies and 11 potential risk factors were included and analysed, with results indicating that eight characteristics—age, presence of symptoms, non-sustained VT, LV origin, epicardial origin, interpolation, PVC duration, and PVC burden—were significantly linked to the development of PVC-CM. Two meta-analyses examining PVC-CM and ablation outcomes were published in 2014. Zang et al . included data from 15 studies involving 712 patients and reported a mean PVC burden of 24% prior to ablation, along with an overall mean increase in LVEF of 7.7% following ablation (12.4% in patients with baseline LV dysfunction). These findings led to the conclusion that ablation of frequent PVCs improves cardiac function, particularly in patients with impaired LVEF. The second meta-analysis, conducted by Lamba and colleagues, 88 focused on PVCs originating from the RVOT and analysed results from six studies. Ablation in this subgroup significantly reduced PVC burden and improved LVEF by a mean of 10.36%. Although strong evidence now supports catheter ablation as an effective intervention for improving EF in PVC-CM, some data suggest that comparable benefits may also be achieved with pharmacological therapy, provided that suppression of PVC burden is equally successful. 89

PVC burden, PVC morphology, and other electrophysiological features In addition to studies evaluating the effects on cardiac function and clinical outcomes, some investigations have focused on risk stratification of patients with PVCs based on electrophysiological characteristics. Several authors have used a series of such features to construct risk scores for PVC patients. 90 The question of whether a threshold exists in the number of PVCs has been examined in multiple studies, with inconsistent findings. Notably, a lower-than-expected PVC burden has occasionally been associated with poorer prognosis. 52 , 91–94 Using receiver operating characteristic curves, Lin et al. identified 12 PVCs per day as the (surprisingly low) optimal cut-off value for increased risk of heart failure and sudden death, 51 with sensitivity and specificity values of approximately 60%. However, other studies have failed to demonstrate a clear correlation between PVC burden and clinical outcomes. 53

Broad PVCs, defined by the width of the QRS complex during the ectopic contraction, have been linked to adverse prognosis, with an approximate cut-off value of 150 millisecond. 95–99 A wide QRS during PVCs may serve both as a risk marker and a risk factor: impaired myocardial conduction can reflect underlying fibrotic tissue, while slow depolarization itself can lead to dyssynchrony. Furthermore, wider PVCs may indicate an epicardial origin. PVC morphology—used as a surrogate for site of origin—has also been investigated as a tool for risk stratification. Evidence in this area appears more robust among individuals with established heart disease, in whom multifocal PVCs are associated with worse outcomes compared to unifocal. 55 , 100 , 101 In contrast, for structurally healthy individuals with PVCs, the prognostic significance of QRS morphology remains uncertain. A notable limitation is that most relevant studies have been conducted in ablation or other settings involving highly selected patient populations. 91 , 96 , 102–106

Other electrophysiological parameters evaluated include PVC interpolation, coupling interval, and the Peak Deflection Index 95 , 99 , 107 , 108 . With respect to the coupling interval, both long- and short-coupled PVCs have been reported to trigger malignant ventricular arrhythmia. 95 , 109 , 110 This apparent discrepancy may be explained by distinct mechanisms: short coupling intervals are more likely to initiate malignant arrhythmias, whereas long intervals may increase the risk of left ventricular dysfunction. Another hypothesis suggests that pronounced rhythm irregularity itself—characterized by both long and short intervals (high ‘interval dispersion’)—serves as a predictor of cardiomyopathy. 111

Diagnostics and significance of imaging findings Current guidelines recommend a comprehensive evaluation of patients with ventricular arrhythmia, including assessment of individual and family history, physical examination, 12-lead ECG, ambulatory electrocardiography, and exercise testing. Nevertheless, in clinical practice, not all patients with PVCs undergo the full range of examinations necessary to exclude structural heart disease.

An unresolved issue is whether conventional imaging techniques are sufficiently accurate to detect subtle abnormalities, such as small areas of myocardial damage that may serve as the origin of PVCs, or whether more advanced imaging modalities should be employed. CMR has gained increasing recognition in recent years as a valuable tool for identifying subtle forms of heart disease in patients with PVCs. A pioneering study by Proclemer in 1997 reported findings from CMR examinations of 19 patients with frequent monomorphic PVCs and 10 controls. 112 The results demonstrated that RVOT dimensions were larger in PVC patients, and wall motion abnormalities were present in 16 of 19 cases, whereas all controls exhibited normal MRI findings. These observations were subsequently confirmed by several studies, 59 , 113–116 some of which also established a link between CMR findings and prognostic outcomes. 117 , 118 A particularly noteworthy study by Nucifora, 119 included 46 patients with monomorphic ventricular arrhythmia of LV origin and 74 patients with idiopathic monomorphic arrhythmia of RV origin, divided into two groups. The LV group exhibited significantly more CMR abnormalities, which were also associated with adverse cardiac events. CMR has further been applied for aetiological diagnosis in populations with and without previously characterized mixed ventricular arrhythmias 120 , 121 and to elucidate the differential contribution of PVCs to haemodynamic function. 122 , 123 Despite these advances, most studies have employed narrow inclusion criteria regarding PVC morphology, PVC burden 124 or other patient characteristics. Consequently, important questions remain about the broader applicability of CMR in the evaluation of PVC patients.

Although CMR is recommended in both European and American guidelines, and its role is generally more clearly highlighted in 2022 guidelines, 29 the method is not broadly used in clinical praxis. This is partially due to its cost and limited accessibility. Echocardiography, on the other hand, is a more common evaluation method, and it has been studied whether additional echocardiographic parameters can add clinically relevant information. However, the body of literature in this field is not as large as for CMR. We have already mentioned the study by Lie about the burden of PVCs leading to PVC-CM. 92 This study used speckle tracking echocardiography to assess left ventricular global longitudinal strain (GLS) and mechanical dispersion and stated that PVC burden correlated with GLS and mechanical dispersion but not with ejection fraction. Other studies have used speckle-tracking echocardiography to identify subtle myocardial dysfunction in PVC patients. In the study from Wijnmaalen, 125 49 subjects with PVCs and 26 healthy controls had normal LVEF; however, speckle tracking showed reduced ventricular strain significantly more often in PVC cases than in controls. Radial, circumferential, and longitudinal strain improved significantly after ablation but remained unchanged in untreated patients. Ling studied 40 subjects with monomorphic frequent PVCs and 40 control 126 and detected no significant differences in standard 2D-echocardiographical findings (including EF) between the two groups; however, parameters evaluated with 3D speckle tracking echocardiography were significantly worse in the PVC group. While most studies have primarily concentrated on systolic LV function, others have adopted a broader perspective, investigating echocardiographic measures of the impact of PVCs on right ventricular, atrial, and diastolic left ventricular function, 127 , 128 as well as how these parameters are influenced by successful catheter ablation. 129

Indications for PVC suppression In most cases, treatment aimed at suppressing premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) is unnecessary, as PVCs are often asymptomatic or too infrequent to produce significant symptoms or adversely affect ventricular structure or function. When the daily PVC burden is low (i.e. fewer than 10 000 PVCs per day, corresponding to approximately 10% of total daily beats), therapy is generally deferred.

In patients with structurally normal hearts, the decision to treat PVCs should be guided primarily by symptom burden and, critically, by a clear correlation between symptoms and PVCs documented on ECG recordings. This correlation is essential because many patients report nonspecific symptoms, such as fatigue or reduced exercise tolerance, which may be related to PVCs due functional bradysphygmia and relative hypoperfusion, but also to other non-arrhythmia related mechanism(s). Therefore, establishing a symptom-ECG correlation helps determine whether PVCs are truly responsible for the symptoms and allows to set realistic expectations regarding the benefits of PVC suppressive therapy.

A higher PVC burden (>10–15%) has been associated with the development of left ventricular dysfunction in patients with previously structurally normal hearts, as well as with worsening ventricular function in those with underlying cardiomyopathy. Consequently, PVC suppression is generally recommended when there is clinical suspicion that frequent PVCs are causing or contributing to left ventricular dysfunction. Similarly, in patients with cardiac resynchronization therapy devices, frequent PVCs may reduce effective biventricular pacing. In such cases, PVC suppression has been shown to restore adequate pacing percentages and promote favourable left ventricular remodelling.

Finally, PVCs may serve as triggers for ventricular fibrillation, particularly when they are short-coupled (occurring at or before the peak of the T wave) or originate from the fascicular/Purkinje system. In these scenarios, interventions aimed at PVC suppression can be life-saving.

Therapeutic approaches for PVC suppression PVC suppression can be achieved with either pharmacologic therapy (e.g. antiarrhythmic drugs, AADs) or catheter ablation. Catheter ablation is recommended by international expert consensus documents in patients with frequent and symptomatic PVCs, whenever AADs are ineffective, not tolerated, or not preferred. In select cases where the putative site of origin of the PVC is more favourably amenable to catheter ablation, such as the right ventricular outflow tract, it is reasonable to prefer catheter ablation over AADs as a first-line therapy.

Antiarrhythmic drugs Clinical data on efficacy and safety of AAD therapy for PVC mostly derive from small non-controlled studies, with efficacy assessed with inconsistent and limited follow-up ECG monitoring. Beta blockers are often used as first-line therapy for symptomatic PVCs, although evidence of efficacy is scant with studies documenting clinically significant PVC count reduction in less than 25% of patients. 130 , 131 Similarly, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are widely used for PVC suppression in patients with structurally normal heart, although data on efficacy of these agents are mostly limited to PVCs of fascicular/Purkinje origin. 132 , 133 However, given the significant negative inotropic effect of non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, these agents are avoided in patients with LV dysfunction. Class IC AADs, and particularly flecainide, are among the most effective AADs to suppress PVCs with demonstrated efficacy in reducing PVC burden in patients with and without underlying cardiomyopathy. 89 , 134 However, particular caution should be exercised when prescribing these agents in patients with underlying cardiomyopathic substrates and left ventricular dysfunction given the documented risk of pro-arrhythmia and the associated negative inotropic effect that can worsen underlying heart failure. 135 , 136

Class III AADs (amiodarone, sotalol) have been formally tested in randomized controlled trials for prevention of sustained ventricular arrhythmias in patients with structural heart disease, 137 , 138 but not specifically for PVC suppression. Considering the potential for significant side effects associated with the use of class III AADs, 139 the use of these agents should be mostly reserved for patients with underlying cardiomyopathic substrates and frequent PVCs for which catheter ablation may be associated with significant risks, such as PVCs originating adjacent to the proximal conduction system (e.g. para-Hisian origin) or major coronary arteries (e.g. septal LV summit region), or in patients with high burden of multifocal PVCs without a predominant morphology amenable to mapping and ablation.

Catheter ablation of PVCs: general considerations The ideal candidates for catheter ablation of PVCs are those with frequent ventricular ectopy from a single predominant focus. 140 , 141 In these cases, it can be reasonably expected to be able to localize with high accuracy the site of origin of PVCs with mapping, and a meaningful burden reduction (or complete abolition) of PVCs following catheter ablation can be anticipated. In patients with high burden of multifocal PVCs, it is important to identify whether there are dominant (i.e. frequent and monomorphic) morphologies that may be amenable to mapping and ablation; in the absence of a clear dominant PVC morphology or cluster of morphologies that may originate from a single distinct anatomical site(e.g. papillary muscle, interventricular septum—see also below), mapping and ablation is challenging and AADs are the most appropriate strategy to suppress PVCs. 140 , 141 In this context, in patients with PVCs who are being considered for catheter ablation, obtaining a 12-lead ECG of the PVCs is of crucial importance owing to its high spatial accuracy in determining the PVC site of origin, particularly in patients with structurally normal heart. Several ECG algorithms have been described to aid preprocedural localization of PVCs, 142–145 with some involving relatively cumbersome ECG measurements. Previous publications have provided excellent ECG-examples that can be used in this process. 146 From a practical standpoint, the most relevant ECG characteristics to guide procedural approaches and anticipate mapping/ablation complexity are the following ( Figure 2 ):

The QRS axis in the frontal plane. An inferior QRS axis (i.e. predominantly positive forces in the inferior leads II, III, aVF) indicates an origin from the superior base of the heart (i.e. outflow tract or superior aspect of atrioventricular valves). On the other hand, a superior QRS axis (i.e. predominantly negative forces in the inferior leads) indicates origin from the diaphragmatic aspect of the ventricles. Furthermore, the axis deviation (i.e. right vs. left) corroborates origin from the left ventricle (right axis) vs. right ventricle (left axis).

The precordial QRS transition zone is helpful in determining basal vs. apical origin. In RBBB pattern PVCs, a progressively later transition zone indicates more basal ventricular origin. In LBBB pattern PVCs, a later transition zone indicates origin towards the free wall of the RV whereas more septal origin are associated with progressively earlier transition zones. Total QRS width: septal sites of origin have narrower QRS widths compared to free wall sites.

Noninvasive ECG imaging tools have been developed with the main aim of improving preprocedural recognition of the putative site of origin of focal arrhythmias, including PVCs. While some systems use information from the 12-lead ECG to project on a three-dimensional heart model the putative PVC site of origin based on automated vector analysis (Vektor Medical, San Diego, California), 147 other systems derive information from dedicated multielectrode vests applied to the patient’s torso to project the local activation onto a three-dimensional geometry of the heart obtained with preacquired chest computer tomography. 148 To date, the real clinical advantage of these more advanced noninvasive ECG imaging solutions over information derived from analysis of 12-lead ECG utilizing established criteria is largely unproven.

Invasive cardiac mapping remains the most accurate method to identify the PVC site of origin. In general, invasive mapping consists of two main approaches, namely: activation mapping and pace-mapping. Activation mapping is the preferred technique, but it requires PVCs to have a sufficient intraprocedural burden to allow for adequate localization. 149 The main goal of activation mapping is to identify the intracardiac earliest activation site in relation to the onset of the PVC QRS; this requires point-by-point analysis of the local activation time with rowing intracardiac catheters. Currently, multipolar large-footprint catheters incorporating multiple small electrodes with tight interelectrode space and covering a larger surface area compared to conventional small-tip mapping and radiofrequency ablation catheters represent the gold standard technology for identification of near-field cardiac activation, although obtaining adequate contact with cardiac regions that are commonly implicated in idiopathic PVCs such as the perivalvular myocardium or intracavitary papillary muscles may be challenging.

For patients with infrequent PVCs and to further corroborate findings from activation mapping, pace-mapping is commonly utilized, with the aim of reproducing the exact 12-lead ECG morphology of the target PVC by pacing from different cardiac sites with a rowing catheter. 150 , 151 Current generation mapping software is able to automatically compare the 12-lead ECG of spontaneous PVCs with QRS derived from pace-mapping creating a ‘match’ score. Typically, a score >0.9 (i.e. >90% QRS pattern match) is considered a good pace match.

Common sites of origin of PVCs: implications for mapping and ablation PVC sites of origin tend to cluster to specific cardiac regions, such as the perivalvular myocardial tissue (e.g. outflow tract in proximity to the aortic/pulmonary valves or perimitral/peritricuspid valve), intracavitary structures such as the papillary muscles and moderator band, and, more rarely, from the Purkinje network. With the exception of PVCs from the Purkinje network and intracavitary structures which are, by definition, targeted only with an endocardial approach, perivalvular PVCs may require endocardial, epicardial or direct intramural mapping (via venous or arterial septal perforators, when available) depending on their site of origin.

Outflow tract PVCs The ventricular outflow tracts are the most common sites of origin of idiopathic PVCs. 141 , 152 Historically, the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) has been reported as the most common site of origin of idiopathic PVCs, 153 although more recent case series have documented an increase in prevalence of left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) PVCs. 152 As septal outflow tract PVCs are by far the most common type of PVCs referred for catheter ablation, 154 the reported increase in prevalence of LVOT PVCs may reflect an increased awareness of the importance of systematic mapping of both right and left outflow tracts, with resulting improved intraprocedural identification of LVOT sources.

Outflow tract PVCs are invariably characterized by an inferior QRS axis—analysis of the relative forces in leads II and III is helpful to distinguish right (R wave in II greater than III) vs. left (R wave in III greater than II) outflow tract origin. As aforementioned, QRS width and transition zone are also helpful to distinguish between different sites around the right and left ventricular outflow tracts, with wider QRS durations indicating non-septal origin, and an RBBB pattern or LBBB with early (before V4) transition more typical of LVOT origin. Unless ECG criteria clearly indicate an LVOT focus, intraprocedural activation mapping is typically carried out sequentially from the RVOT and moving to the LVOT in case of early septal activation, particularly in the presence of a broad area of similarly early activation ( Figure 3 ). Pace-mapping is mostly useful for non-septal outflow tract locations, although the presence of preferential conduction within the outflow tract, together with the suboptimal spatial resolution of 12-lead ECG, should be taken into consideration when using pace-mapping to localize the putative site of origin of outflow tract PVCs. 155 , 156

The outcomes of catheter ablation of outflow tract PVCs are generally good, but success rates are variable, which reflects the anatomical complexity of this region. For classical outflow tract VAs accessible with an endocardial approach, such as those from the endocardial outflow tract (RVOT or LVOT) or those easily accessible from the aortic/pulmonary cusp region, ablation outcomes have been reported as excellent (>90% efficacy in PVC suppression). 131 , 157 One important safety consideration when targeting outflow tract PVCs from the aortic or pulmonic cusp region is the potential proximity to the proximal coronary arteries. Intraprocedural imaging with intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) has been shown to be very reliable in localizing the position of the mapping/ablation catheter in relationship to the proximal coronary arteries, 158 thus preventing the need for intraprocedural angiography. However, in centres where ICE is not available or if the operator is not proficient with the use of ICE to localize the proximal coronary arteries, intraprocedural coronary angiography should be considered when targeting outflow tract arrhythmias from the aortic or pulmonary cusp region.

An important subset of outflow tract PVCs may have an intramural site of origin. 159–162 Indirect clues for intramural PVC origin include a similar broad area of early activation on both sides of the interventricular septum (or endo-epicardially), lack of a distinct QS unipolar electrogram pattern at the earliest endocardial or epicardial site, and lack of good pace-match from accessible endocardial or epicardial sites. 160 , 161 Whenever possible, direct intramural mapping via accessible septal perforators of the venous (preferred approach) or arterial system can confirm an intramural origin by proving earliest intramural activation. 159 In most of these cases, catheter ablation can be performed from anatomically adjacent endocardial (or aortic/pulmonary cusp) sites provided that the anatomical distance between the earliest intramural site and the adjacent endocardial site is within 8–10 mm. 159 , 163 , 164 If conventional unipolar radiofrequency ablation fails, bailout strategies such as bipolar radiofrequency ablation, irrigated ablation utilizing a lowered ionic irrigant (i.e. half-normal saline), ethanol ablation from within the septal perforators ( Figure 4 ) or, more recently, pulsed field ablation (PFA) have been used to increase lesion depth and enhance procedural success. 165–167

Perimitral and peritricuspid PVCs The myocardial tissue at the perimitral or peritricuspid ventricular ostia is also a common site of origin of idiopathic PVCs. Perimitral PVCs have a typical RBBB pattern (unless arising from the most septal aspect of the annulus where they may also display a LBBB pattern) and right axis deviation, whereas peritricuspid PVCs always display a LBBB pattern and left axis deviation. The polarity of the QRS complexes in the frontal plane depends on the PVC site of origin along the mitral or tricuspid annuli (i.e. PVCs from the superior portion of the mitral/tricuspid annulus will have an inferior axis, whereas PVCs from the inferior portion of the mitral/tricuspid annulus will have a superior axis). Unlike outflow tract PVCs, which are typically observed in patients with no underlying structural heart disease, a subset of patients with perimitral or peritricuspid PVCs may have an associated concealed cardiomyopathy, especially if PVCs are multifocal. 168 , 169 Mitral annular PVCs most commonly arise from the superior portion of the mitral annulus, 170 and, similarly to outflow tract PVCs, may originate from the subendocardium, epicardium, or mid-myocardium. Mapping is usually performed from the endocardium and/or epicardium via the coronary sinus, as direct percutaneous epicardial mapping has a low yield due to the presence of coronary arteries and epicardial fat around the atrioventricular groove. Peritricuspid PVCs account for up to 8% of idiopathic PVCs, and most commonly arise from the septal aspect of the annulus. 171 Catheter stability during mapping and ablation of the ventricular aspect of the tricuspid annulus can be challenging owing to the beat-to-beat anteroposterior motion of the annulus together with increased susceptibility to respiratory catheter drift. In general, the success rate of catheter ablation of free wall peritricuspid PVCs has been reported higher compared to septal locations, 171 possibly related to the frequent intramural origin and/or proximity to the proximal conduction system (i.e. para-Hisian location, see also below) of some septal peritricuspid PVCs.

PVCs from intracavitary structures Intracavitary structures, including the left and right ventricular papillary muscles and the moderator band, are a recognized source of idiopathic PVCs, although they occur far less commonly than perivalvular PVCs. 172–175 In contrast, among patients with PVC-triggered ventricular fibrillation, intracavitary sites and the Purkinje network represent some of the most frequent sites of origin. 176 , 177 Papillary Muscle PVCs tend to have a focal, non-reentrant mechanism tied to abnormal automaticity or triggered activity. Rather than being induced by programmed stimulation, they are generally exercise-related and brought on by catecholamine surges. 178

In the first description by the University of Alabama group in 2008, out of 290 consecutive patients referred for catheter ablation of idiopathic PVCs or VT, 7 (2.4%) were identified with a site of origin at the postero-medial papillary muscle (PM-PM). 173 The same group subsequently described another series of six patients with focal ventricular arrhythmias where the site of origin was identified at the anterolateral papillary muscle (AL-PM). 175 Following this initial description, ventricular arrhythmias from intracavitary structures have been increasingly recognized and described by other groups, 170 , 172 , 174 , 179 including right ventricular papillary muscles and moderator band sources. 180 , 181 LV papillary muscle PVCs have a characteristic RBBB pattern with relatively short intrinsicoid deflection time (<74 ms) and mid-wall transition (V3-V4). 182 The frontal plane axis depends on the origin: PM-PM typically displays a left superior axis, whereas AL-PM displays a right inferior axis with characteristic inferior lead ‘discordance’ (i.e. negative in lead II, positive in lead III). RV papillary muscle and moderator band sources have a LBBB pattern with a typical left superior axis (more negative in III than II) and late (>V5) transition. 181 Mapping and catheter ablation of PVCs originating from intracavitary structures can be challenging owing to the complex anatomy and mobile nature of the papillary muscles during the cardiac cycle. Intraprocedural ICE imaging has proven invaluable for defining the anatomy of the papillary muscles/moderator band, monitoring for catheter-tissue contact, and validating complete sampling around the complex geometry of these structures ( Figure 5 ). 172 , 174 , 176 , 180–183 Overall, catheter ablation of PVCs from intracavitary structures has been shown safe but less effective compared to the more typical outflow tract sites, with success rates ranging from 80% to 92% and more frequent need for multiple ablation procedures. 184 This is largely related to inability to deliver adequate radiofrequency lesions at the target site due to challenges in obtaining and maintaining adequate tissue-catheter contact—in this context, the use of contact force sensing catheter technologies is helpful to validate adequate contact. In order to overcome these limitations, cryoablation has been utilized successfully in cases where radiofrequency has failed. 185–187 One important advantage of cryoablation over radiofrequency ablation for intracavitary structures is the tissue-catheter adherence and, hence, stability after reaching cryoablation temperatures (<−70°C). 185–187

PVCs from epicardial locations Approximately 4–10% of patients with idiopathic PVCs have epicardial sites of origin, 152 , 188 with the most common site being the perivalvular LVOT epicardium, a region commonly referred to as the LV summit being the most superior aspect of the LV epicardium. 189–191 The LV summit is bordered by the bifurcation of the left anterior descending (LAD) and left circumflex (LCx) coronary arteries, and laterally crossed by the great cardiac vein (GCV) at its junction with the anterior interventricular vein (AIV) ( Figure 5 ). 189–191 The course of the GCV divides the LV summit into two regions: a medial, more superior area above the GCV that is generally not amenable to direct catheter ablation because of its close proximity to major coronary arteries and the presence of thick epicardial fat (the ‘inaccessible’ region), and a more lateral, inferior area below the GCV that may be directly reachable with ablation because it lies farther from the main coronary vessels (the ‘accessible’ region). Several ECG markers have been proposed to identify PVCs arising from the LV summit and to help distinguish whether the focus originates from the accessible or inaccessible portion, which can guide procedural strategy. 189 , 192 LV summit arrhythmias display either a RBBB pattern with positive concordance across the precordial leads, or a LBBB pattern with an early (≤V2) precordial transition with characteristic right inferior axis. Additional ECG clues to epicardial origin include slurring at the onset of the QRS complex which reflects slow epicardial-to-endocardial conduction and this can be quantified using the following criteria: (i) pseudo-delta wave (time to earliest rapid deflection in the precordial leads) ≥34 ms, (ii) intrinsicoid deflection time in V2 (interval to peak R wave) ≥85 ms, (iii) maximum deflection index (MDI: shortest interval to maximal deflection divided by QRS duration) ≥0.55, and (iv) shortest RS complex (time to earliest QRS nadir in precordial leads) ≥121 ms. 189 , 191 , 193 Anatomically opposite to the LV summit is the ‘cardiac crux’, which is the most posterior and inferior epicardial region of the LV adjacent to the epicardial RV inferior base ( Figure 5 ). In this region, the posterior atrioventricular and interventricular grooves meet near the origin of the middle cardiac vein (MCV) from the coronary sinus (CS). Idiopathic PVCs from the crux/MCV typically show an LBBB pattern with transition ≤V2, a left superior axis with QS and slurred inferior-lead deflections, and an MDI ≥0.55. Procedurally, the crux can be divided into a basal portion (often ablated from the MCV or proximal CS) and an apical portion (which may require subxiphoid epicardial access). 194

Catheter ablation of epicardial PVCs is challenging as direct ablation at the earliest site of origin is often not possible due to proximity to major coronary arteries or presence of epicardial fat, as aforementioned. 164 , 189 , 194 An anatomical approach targeting adjacent and accessible vantage points is typically adopted to target these arrhythmias, with variable success rates (ranging from 50% to 80%) largely depending on the anatomical distance between the epicardial site of origin and the adjacent target site. 164 , 190 , 191 For LV summit arrhythmias, common adjacent mapping and ablation vantage points include the coronary cusp region, the LVOT perivalvular endocardium, the antero-septal RVOT and the distal GCV/AIV. An anatomical ablation approach is most effective when adjacent targets are ≤12.8 mm apart or when their local activation times differ by ≤7 ms. 164 , 195 , 196 Prolonged radiofrequency applications (3–5 min) have with gradual power escalation up to 40 Watts have been associated with improved long-term PVC suppression. 197

PVCs linked to the conduction system (para-Hisian, Purkinje-related) Between 3% and 9% of idiopathic PVCs originate in the basal upper septum in proximity to the His bundle region. 198 , 199 Para-Hisian PVCs have specific ECG features including a LBBB pattern with QS pattern in V1 and early precordial transition (V2-V3), narrow QRS duration indicating septal origin, monophasic R waves in lead I reflecting right-to-left LV activation, and a characteristic ‘inferior lead discordance’ with predominant positive (or more positive) forces in lead II and more negative in lead III. 198–200 As catheter ablation at the earliest Para-Hisian site is associated with a substantial risk of collateral injury to the conduction system, these arrhythmias are best approached from anatomically adjacent vantage points such as the posterior coronary cusp region (right coronary cusp and its junction with the non-coronary cusp). 198 When ablation from these sites is unsuccessful, direct ablation at the earliest site can be considered, although the risk of periprocedural injury to the conduction system may be significant in these cases. Purkinje-related PVCs originate from ramifications of the right and left bundle branches, and are commonly implicated in VF triggers both in patients with structurally normal hearts and in patients with underlying cardiomyopathic states. 201–203 ECG morphologies associated with Purkinje PVCs typically replicate focal antegrade activation along the fascicle of origin (although different degrees of fusion due to retrograde invasion of the other fascicles is possible), with PVCs originating from the RBB and its ramification displaying an LBBB morphology and PVCs originating from the LBB a RBBB morphology with either right inferior (left anterior fascicle origin) or left superior (left posterior fascicle origin) axis. Catheter ablation targeting the earliest Purkinje potentials has been shown to be highly effective in suppressing Purkinje-related PVCs, 201 and abolishing episodes of recurrent VF in up to 80% of cases. 204

Catheter ablation energy sources for PVCs: current standards and future directions Open irrigated radiofrequency ablation remains the current standard of care for targeting idiopathic PVCs, with an excellent track record of safety and efficacy. As aforementioned, lesion depth with conventional small-tip irrigated RF remains its main limitation, particularly when targeting intramural foci or mobile structures where tissue-catheter contact is poor and/or intermittent. Bailout ablation strategies have been described with the main purpose of increasing the lesion depth in challenging PVC locations. These include direct intramural tissue chemical ablation with alcohol injection within a venous or arterial septal perforator, bipolar radiofrequency ablation, ablation utilizing lower ionic irrigation, cryoablation (for intracavitary structures), and pulsed field ablation (PFA). 159 , 165 , 167 , 205 The latter represent a particularly promising technology given the more selective nonthermal ablation with potential for lower risk of collateral damage to adjacent tissues. 206 , 207 Additional advantages include better lesion depth and penetration through scar as compared to radiofrequency ablation. 208 In a randomized preclinical study, 209 Younis et al . compared contact force sensing open irrigated radiofrequency ablation with monopolar PFA in common idiopathic PVC locations including the LVS region (targeted from the distal GCV/AIV), the LV papillary muscles and direct epicardial ablation (75% of cases with interposed epicardial fat). Overall, PFA outperformed radiofrequency ablation lesion depth in all tested locations, 209 suggesting that this ablation technology may offer real additive advantages over radiofrequency ablation for challenging idiopathic PVC sites. On the other hand, the risk of PFA-induced coronary vasospasm when targeting sites adjacent to major coronary arteries remains a concern for perivalvular PVC ablation. 210 , 211 Thus far, the clinical experience with PFA for idiopathic PVC ablation is still early and limited to small case series. Additional investigation is needed to determine the role of PFA for idiopathic PVC ablation. In particular, prospective multicentre studies and randomized controlled trials comparing PFA with RF are warranted. Beyond acute procedural success, future studies should evaluate long-term arrhythmia-free survival, lesion durability, procedural efficiency, quality-of-life outcomes, and the impact on ventricular function. Furthermore, as lesion characteristics and safety profiles may vary according to PVC origin and anatomical substrate, dedicated studies are needed across different ventricular locations. Such investigations will be essential to define the optimal indications, safety, efficacy, and potential advantages of PFA within the evolving landscape of PVC ablation.

In the management of refractory PVCs, several advanced strategies exist beyond standard RF ablation. For papillary muscle PVCs, cryoablation provides better catheter stability, translating into higher rates of acute success and fewer recurrences compared to RF. 186 When foci are intramural, deeper lesions can be achieved through approaches such as bipolar ablation 212 needle ablation, or irrigation with half-normal saline. 167

Conclusions and future perspectives PVCs are so commonly encountered that they have been defined as ‘ubiquitous’ 213 and even as ‘the incidentalomas of cardiac electrophysiology’. 214 Despite their frequency, their prognostic significance, associated morbidity, and optimal management remain subjects of ongoing debate. Because PVCs can appear in a wide range of individuals—including older patients with cardiac or noncardiac comorbidities, many of whom are asymptomatic—any decision to pursue further diagnostic evaluation must be guided by general medical and ethical principles, with the goal of determining whether additional testing is likely to benefit the patient. When a diagnostic work–up is undertaken, its primary objective should be to identify or exclude underlying structural heart disease. In patients without structural abnormalities, management should focus on assessing future risk, considering PVC burden, morphology, and other electrocardiographic characteristics. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging, particularly the detection of myocardial fibrosis, has demonstrated prognostic value. Treatment of PVCs is typically symptom–driven, yet therapy may also be considered in asymptomatic individuals when reduction of PVC burden is desirable. Catheter ablation is generally more effective than pharmacologic therapy for PVC suppression.

In recent years, new technologies for rhythm monitoring have emerged. Smartphones and smartwatches can now detect PVCs using photoplethysmography–based algorithms 215 a development that will likely increase the identification of incidental PVCs. This trend underscores the need for evidence–based decision–making to avoid unnecessary interventions. At the same time, ensuring access to advanced diagnostic and therapeutic tools—such as CMR, genetic testing, and invasive electrophysiologic studies—remains essential for the appropriate application of current scientific knowledge.

The pathophysiology of VT is multifactorial in nature and often categorized and treated according to the presence of underlying heart disease (e.g. ischaemic or structural heart disease). 3 , 4 Albeit VT is considered important in terms of morbidity, mortality, and societal expenses, reliable population-based data regarding contemporary incidence and treatment are sparse outside the limitations of selected cohorts. 5 Hence, using nationwide Danish data, we sought to investigate temporal trends in incidence, treatment patterns, as well as prognosis in patients with VT.

Methods In Denmark, it is possible to link multiple clinical registries enabling follow-up on an individual level (e.g. hospital diagnoses, surgical and interventional procedures, prescriptions dispensed at pharmacies). The registries have been described in detail elsewhere. 6–8

First, an analysis was designed to describe temporal patterns in the incidence of new-onset VT using the whole adult Danish population as reference. Second, we constructed a cohort of adult patients (≥ 18 years and ≤100 years of age) defined by a first-time diagnosis of VT. Ventricular tachycardia was defined by first-time diagnoses comprising all types of monomorphic VT (including re-entry VT), idiopathic VT, as well as VT without further specification between 2011 and 2023.

The primary factors of interest were early catheter ablation, implantable cardioverter defibrillator treatment (ICD implantation), as well as pharmacological treatment with anti-arrhythmic drugs (AADs) and beta-blockers within 180 days (time of follow-up initiation). Anti-arrhythmic drugs in question were amiodarone, class 1c AADs, sotalol, and dronedarone. The clinical outcome of interest was all-cause mortality.

The annual incidence of VT [incidence rates (IR)] was calculated as the counts of incident diagnoses per 100 000 individuals per year during the study period (2011–23) and depicted graphically with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). Temporal trends in the proportion of patients with therapeutic interventions (catheter ablation, ICD implantation, AADs) were depicted graphically. The absolute risk of all-cause mortality was calculated using the Aalen–Johansen estimator.

Results The annual IR of VT remained relatively stable from 2011 until 2023 with a slight tendency towards decreased VT incidence over time (IR 21, 95% CI 20–23 per 100 000 individuals in 2011 to IR 17, 95% CI 16–18 per 100 000 individuals in 2023) ( Figure 1A ).

Figure 1 ( A ) Incidence rates of VT. The x -axis depicts years during the study period and the y -axis incidence per 100 000 individuals. ( B ) Figure depicting treatment strategies (ICD, ablation, and AADs). The x -axis depicts years during the study period and the y -axis the proportion in percentage (%). ( C ) The absolute risk of all-cause mortality in patients with VT. The blue colour depicts all VT patients, while the red and black colours depict VT patients with and without structural heart disease, respectively. The x -axis depicts time elapsed in years and the y -axis the risk of death in percentage (%).

For image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text. The prevalence of structural heart disease (including ischaemic heart disease) was substantial (69%), with significant ischaemic heart disease (56%), heart failure (44%), valvular heart disease (12%), as well as any diagnosis of a specific cardiomyopathy (17%). The ICD implantation was common (43%) with an increase during the study period (38% in 2011 to 54% in 2023) ( Figure 1B ).

The use of AADs was common (25%), which remained relatively stable, albeit, with a small increase in the most contemporary years. The predominant AAD was amiodarone (24%). Beta-blocker treatment was very common (74%), which was unchanged during the study period. Early catheter ablation increased during the study period (4% in 2011 to 10% in 2023) ( Figure 1B ).

Significant mortality was observed both in the short term (1-year mortality 6.8%, 95% CI 6.3–7.2), intermediate term (5-year mortality 26.1%, 95% CI 25.1–27.1), as well as long term (10-year mortality 43.3%, 95% CI 42.0–44.7) ( Figure 1C ). Moreover, the mortality associated with VT was highly dependent upon underlying structural heart disease. During the study period (2011–23), we found no notable differences in the prognosis following a VT diagnosis as the mortality remained relatively stable (1-year mortality 6.6%, 95% CI 5.0–8.3 in 2012 compared with a 1-year mortality of 6.5%, 95% CI 4.6–8.5 in 2022).

Discussion Rhythm control interventions such as ICD implantation, catheter ablation, and AADs are all established interventions with proven clinical benefits and potential mortality reduction in patients with VT. 9 , 10 Accordingly, these treatments were relatively common in our study with a trend towards increasing use in recent years. The frequent use of AADs, predominantly amiodarone (>30% in some years), could seem unexpected. Given the well-documented efficacy of catheter ablation in reducing VT burden, this could point to a gap between available evidence and contemporary clinical management strategies, as a proportion of patients could potentially benefit from early ablation rather than prolonged exposure to AADs with substantial side-effect profiles. 9

The background for the modest adaptation of early ablation is unknown; however, patient selection, referral pathways, and accumulation of randomized evidence favouring early ablation published only in the later years of the study period could be hypothesized as important factors. Ventricular tachycardia was associated with significant mortality, especially in patients with structural or ischaemic heart disease (i.e. patients with more advanced myocardial substrate and more complex underlying disease), which were very prevalent in our cohort.

In this context, it is noteworthy that despite the broad clinical implementation of modern therapies, the overall prognosis in patients with VT was unchanged during our study period. However, this should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence that contemporary VT therapies are ineffective as ICDs primarily prevent arrhythmic death and catheter ablation reduces arrhythmia burden and ICD therapies. As such, the underlying myocardial disease and the risk of non-arrhythmic mortality remain unaffected. Moreover, changes over time in factors such as case mix and comorbidity burden could potentially have counterbalanced improvements in therapy.

Study limitations were generally inherent to the observational nature of the data with specific limitations such as no available electrocardiographic documentation to classify type of VT (e.g. VT exit site) or duration of VT episodes (sustained vs. non-sustained). Moreover, specific causes of death (i.e. arrhythmic vs. non-arrhythmic deaths) could not be ascertained from the available data.

Conclusively, we found an overall stable VT incidence over time with increasing adoption of ICD implantation and ablation; however, the frequency of early ablation remained modest. Mortality was significant and modified by the presence of structural heart disease, and importantly, the overall prognosis of VT in terms mortality did not change during the study period. Core Tip: In recent years, electrocardiographic monitoring systems have incorporated many technical improvements that solve several of the 24-h Holter monitor limitations. This review provides an update on the different electrocardiographic cardiac monitoring methods currently available, remarking their indications and limitations, to help healthcare professionals appropriately select and use them in the work-up of patients with palpitations.

INTRODUCTION Palpitations are one of the most common reasons for medical consultation and can occur in up to 10% of the population at some point in their lives[ 1 - 3 ]. They tend to worry patients and can affect their quality of life. They are a symptom that is frequently associated with cardiac rhythm disorders, although there are other etiologies[ 4 ] (Table 1 ). In fact, in up to half of the cases, palpitations are not due to a significative arrhythmia[ 2 ]. Having an accurate diagnosis is important to determinate the prognosis, to guide treatment and to plan the patient’s follow-up. In order to have a diagnosis, it is essential to be able to reliably correlate the symptoms with an electrocardiographic record allowing the identification or ruling out of a possible rhythm disorder. However, reaching a diagnosis is not always simple, given that they tend to be transitory symptoms and the patient is asymptomatic at the time of assessment[ 1 , 5 ].

Electrocardiographic monitoring systems are a first-line tool in assessing these patients. The introduction of the 24-h Holter monitor within 60 s was a true revolution and its use rapidly became widespread[ 6 ]. Other than diagnosing palpitations, it has also been an important tool in understanding the physiological cardiac rhythm behavior[ 7 , 8 ] and in the follow-up of patients at risk of cardiovascular disease[ 8 ], in syncope work-up[ 9 - 12 ], in risk stratification of certain patients[ 13 - 16 ] or in the detection of silent arrhythmias[ 8 , 17 - 21 ]. Due to its high availability and probably due to a certain degree of tradition, it is the monitoring system most commonly used by most doctors. However, it has several limitations that reduce its efficiency and diagnostic yield[ 2 , 22 ].

Fortunately, in recent years, in line with the overall technological development that our society has experienced, electrocardiographic monitoring systems have incorporated many technical upgrades allowing for improvement in several of the limitations presented by the 24-h Holter monitor. This evolution of electrocardiogram (ECG) recording systems has occurred in various directions. On the one hand, we have the improvement in the quality and quantity of recordings, such that, at the present time, it is possible to obtain 12-lead ECG traces of excellent quality with increased monitoring time, be it in the form of a continuous recording (which can last up to a month), or in the form of intermittent recordings which can last up to 3 years in the case of implantable recorders[ 8 , 23 - 25 ]. On the other hand, various recording and analysis algorithms have been developed, which allow for many improvements; for example, the automatic analysis of arrhythmias[ 18 , 23 ]. Remote data transmission systems have also been incorporated with multiple designs able to adapt to each patient’s different needs[ 8 , 24 , 26 ].

Unfortunately, these new devices are still not universally incorporated into daily clinical practice, either because they are not included or reimbursed in the healthcare systems, or due to the inertia of healthcare professionals[ 27 ]. In the work-up for palpitations, it is still usual to apply a traditional strategy that is fundamentally based on the use of a 24-h Holter monitor, which has low diagnostic yield on many occasions[ 2 , 22 ]. This lack of yield is due to the fact that the majority of the events to be diagnosed are paroxysmal ones that occur occasionally and unexpectedly. The use of standardized diagnostic protocols with the application of new electrocardiographic monitoring devices has been shown not only to markedly improve the diagnostic yield, but also to be clearly cost efficient[ 2 , 28 - 30 ].

However, it should also be noted that the new devices are not exempt from limitations. Some are related to patient tolerance, either due to the possibility of relative discomfort, the need to wear external devices with electrodes stuck to the skin, or because the implantable devices require a minor surgical procedure, meaning that certain patients may not accept them[ 8 , 24 , 27 ]. Also, the devices continue to record a significant number of artifacts or rhythmic abnormalities that are not pathological or significant, which inefficiently lengthen the interpretation time of the studies and can even saturate the memory of certain devices. In addition, it should be noted that for a suitable diagnosis to be made, not only is it important to have recorded a quality electrocardiographic trace; the latter must also be properly interpreted in the patient’s clinical context, which requires sufficient skill on the part of the healthcare professional interpreting the trace[ 31 ].

The objective of this review is to offer an update on the different monitoring methods currently available, their indications and limitations, to help healthcare professionals appropriately select and use them in the work-up of patients with palpitations.

ELECTROCARDOGRAPHIC CARDIAC MONITORING DEVICES Device classification The monitoring devices available on the market have differing characteristics. Traditionally, these devices have been classified into three or four groups [24/48-h Holter, external prospective event recorders (PERs), loop recorders (LRs)] based on a series of shared characteristics[ 8 , 27 ] (Table 2 ). However, thanks to technical developments in recent years, the devices have gained in functionality and taken on new properties, making it difficult to establish a strict, closed classification. For this reason, some devices will have mixed characteristics between two groups (or will be able to be used in one or other manner according to the patient). Despite this, we should mention some of the most differentiating characteristics allowing a device and specific model to be classified (Figure 1 ). These characteristics must be considered when indicating the device that best suits each patient.

They may, thus, be classified according to the following. (1) Monitoring time. There are short recording devices (24–48 h) that are useful for the examination of symptoms that occur every day or frequently; mid-range recording devices (up to 4 wk) and long recording devices (up to 3–4 years)[ 32 ]. Due to limitations of data storage, when we increase the monitoring time of the devices, they switch from continuous to intermittent recording, as will be discussed later. To achieve appropriate diagnostic yield in the work-up for palpitations, it is essential to adjust the monitoring time to the frequency of the symptoms. This is, without a doubt, one of the main characteristics when selecting a device. (2) Recording type. This is another important characteristic to be kept in mind when selecting the most suitable test for each patient type. On the one hand, continuous recording devices such as Holter monitors make a constant ECG recording that can later be reviewed in its entirety. Continuous recordings avoid information loss since they do not depend on activation by the patient or on arrhythmia detection algorithms. By contrast, tests using intermittent recording are patient-activated or activate automatically according to different arrhythmia detection algorithms. There are two distinct types of device with this characteristic: Loop recorders [external LRs (ELRs) or implantable LRs (ILRs)] and PERs. The main difference between them is the ability of the LR to record the trace both prospectively and retrospectively, allowing us to obtain the trace from the start of the event (which may be important for the precise diagnosis of certain arrhythmias) (Figure 2 ). Similarly, LRs have various algorithms allowing for the automatic recording of certain asymptomatic arrhythmias, which prospective recorders do not allow for, since they are only activated by the patient in the event of symptoms (as such, they are also not useful for syncope work-up)[ 17 , 32 , 33 ]. It should be noted that there are currently certain devices available with continuous recording capacity as well as off-line analysis software with detection algorithms for arrhythmias that present the information in a similar manner to event recorders (although the healthcare professional can review the rest of the recording if this is considered important)[ 19 , 34 , 35 ].

A premature atrial beat that conducts with long PR seems to be the trigger of the SVT. This finding is highly suggestive of atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia. (3) Number of leads. Recordings range from systems with just one lead to full 12-lead ECGs in the devices with the most leads. It is important to keep in mind that, the greater the number of leads, the more memory the device will use. In addition, there will be a greater number of electrodes to be applied by the patient in order for the recording to be made. As such, as a general rule, the devices allowing for long monitoring times offer a limited number of leads. However, having more than one lead is often useful. For example, on occasion, it allows for the clearing up of doubts as to whether a lead is subject to artifacts (Figure 3 ) or to better assess the wave morphology, which is important on certain occasions[ 8 , 36 , 37 ].

There are implantable and external devices. ILRs require a minor surgical procedure, but once the wound has healed, patients do not usually notice them, and they allow for prolonged monitoring[ 17 , 25 ]. (5) Connectivity. The most up-to-date devices incorporate connectivity systems that allow for remote monitoring. Some can even be linked to smartphones, allowing for the easy sharing and sending of recordings via the Internet or Bluetooth[ 26 , 32 , 38 , 39 ]. In addition, some applications have algorithms that offer the patient an instantaneous diagnosis of their arrhythmia (although it is recommended that this is ratified by a healthcare professional)[ 18 , 40 , 41 ]. (6) Automatic algorithms. Different recording and analysis algorithms have been developed in recent years and they have been incorporated into some devices. Most of these algorithms allow for the automatic analysis of arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation (AF), bradycardia, or asystole, but some of them also allow for the filtering out of noise to try to improve recording quality. There are differences between the algorithms that different brands incorporate into their devices. It is important to evaluate not only the algorithms that they provide, but also their sensitivity and specificity for detecting each type of arrhythmia. All of them should have type I and type II errors, but there may be significant differences depending on the device. Therefore, when selecting a monitoring device, physicians should also consider the accuracy of these algorithms. (7) Recording system type used. Initially, most devices used adhesives with electrodes. This is still the most common used format, although others have been developed that can record the cardiac signal, such as patches, belts or vests[ 8 , 24 ]. There are also devices that do not need to be in constant contact with the patient which incorporate electrodes into the recorder’s own case, which are brought close to the skin when a recording is desired[ 42 - 44 ]. (8) Availability of other biological signals. In addition to recording the electrocardiographic trace, some devices have sensors that allow other biological signals to be monitored, such as physical activity, bodily position, oxygen saturation and even the presence of apnea[ 39 , 45 , 46 ].

Main electrocardiographic monitoring devices available As noted above, there is currently a wide variety of monitoring devices offering a combination of characteristics, which makes it difficult to perform a strict classification. However, it is still useful to differentiate certain major groups (Figure 1 and Table 2 ), in the knowledge that certain models may have mixed characteristics between two groups or may be used in different ways as appropriate (e.g., there are devices that can function as a 24-h Holter monitor, a continuous 3-wk Holter or a loop recorder) .

Continuous Holter (24/48-h): This takes its name from the cardiologist Norman J. Holter, who developed this technology in 1961. It is currently the most common technique used in clinical practice[ 47 ]. Currently, most Holter devices consist of a lightweight recorder with a digital memory card and a series of cutaneous electrodes that obtain a continuous ECG recording. They allow for 24-48-h monitoring time in most cases, although there are devices with recording capacities of up to 7 d.

Originally, the recording was made up of only two or three leads and, still today, many tests are carried out in this way. However, as early as 1966, the first 12-lead Holter monitor was developed with a system of 10 electrodes arranged over the patient’s torso. Later on, a simplified five-electrode system was developed (the EASI system) which allowed for the reconstruction of 12 leads with good clinical reliability[ 48 ]. Having 12 leads may be especially important when assessing certain arrhythmias, such as the morphology of ventricular extrasystoles or certain repolarization patterns which may only appear in one specific lead. Torso electrodes avoid possible artifacts and discomfort associated with the positioning of the electrodes on the limbs. However, it should be noted that this arrangement attenuates the amplitude of the inferior leads and generates a slight right cardiac axis deviation[ 48 ], and some recordings obtained with torso leads cannot be considered completely equivalent to standard ECG leads[ 8 ].

After completing the recording, it is transferred into software installed on a computer (and/or a server in the cloud in some of the more advanced devices), which usually allows for an initial automatic analysis identifying the QRS complexes and the R-R interval to offer values such as maximum/minimum rate, histograms of rate or ST segment analysis. Finally, the healthcare professional must review the data to rule out the presence of possible artifacts and interpret the results of the ECG taking into account the patient’s symptom diary[ 47 ].

Holter monitors have demonstrated their utility in identifying arrhythmias in patients with palpitations or syncope with different efficacy values in line with the pretest probability of the population studied and the frequency of the symptoms[ 2 , 22 , 28 ]. In recent years, various case series, including our own[ 2 , 32 ], have shown that the global diagnostic yield of Holter monitors is limited and that, despite the fact that its cost is generally relatively low, its per-diagnosis cost is high[ 22 , 27 , 47 ]. For example, in a transversal study in usual clinical practice carried out by our group, Holter only offered a diagnostic yield of 3.5% for syncope and 16.5% for palpitations. This yield is even lower when the objective is screening for asymptomatic arrhythmias, such as AF in the context of cryptogenic stroke, where the yield can be < 1%[ 32 ].

Among other indications that have been considered, there was risk stratification in certain groups of patients, either through the detection of nonsustained arrhythmias and abnormalities of heart rate variability parameters or dispersion of the QT interval[ 15 , 49 - 53 ]. However, at the present time, few therapeutic decisions are based on Holter findings, perhaps with the exception of the presence of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy[ 15 ], which may be a decisive factor for the implantation of an implantable cardiac defibrillator.

In our opinion, in the work-up for palpitations at the present time, the 24/48-h Holter monitor should only be considered in patients with daily or very frequent symptoms. When this is not the case, there are other tools available that offer not only a greater diagnostic yield, but also better cost efficiency[ 2 , 39 , 54 ].

Skin patches: These systems, which were developed over the past decade, enjoy a certain degree of popularity in some countries. However, in others, such as Spain, their use remains marginal. They consist of patches of different materials, which adhere to the skin and contain electrodes to obtain one (the most common) or two ECG leads for 7–14 d’ monitoring. The device itself acquires, amplifies and filters the ECG signal, which is then telematically transmitted for analysis (usually through an external company)[ 8 , 24 , 55 ].

There are different patch models with different recording characteristics. In some cases, they are similar to a Holter monitor and in others to an ELR. For example, the ZioPatch creates a continuous ECG recording with a single lead that is interpreted via an analysis platform. It also has a symptom button on the patch itself[ 56 , 57 ]. Another different example is the NUVANT-Piix. It also has only one lead, but it does not perform a continuous recording; rather, it only records the traces identified as arrhythmias or when the patient experiences symptoms and activates the device with a special magnet[ 58 ].

There are studies comparing the efficacy of these new patches with traditional Holter monitors (Table 3 ), showing good tolerability on the part of patients and a greater diagnostic yield, particularly for the purposes of identifying paroxysmal AF[ 56 , 59 ]. However, these devices have a higher cost and are usually single use[ 8 , 56 ].
